fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is a question I think about a lot, and honestly the first thing I'd say is that the question itself is kind of underspecified. People use "world model" to mean very different things. Sometimes they mean something like, does the model have an internal representation of the state of some environment that it's tracking and updating. Sometimes they mean something much looser, like, does the model know facts about how the world works. And those are really different claims, so when someone asks "does GPT have a world model," I usually want to ask back, which one are you talking about?

The way I tend to approach it is to try to make it operational. So you pick a domain where you actually know what the ground-truth state is, and then you ask whether the model's behavior, or its internal activations, are consistent with tracking that state. The classic example people point to is the Othello work, where you train a model only on sequences of moves, nothing else, and then you probe the hidden states and you find you can linearly decode the board. And more importantly, if you intervene on that representation, the model's next-move predictions change in the way they should. That's a pretty convincing result to me, because it's not just correlation, you're actually editing the thing and the behavior follows.

But I'd be careful about generalizing from that. Othello is a tiny, closed world. The rules are fully determined by the data. When you move to natural language, the "world" is enormous and the text is a very lossy, biased projection of it. So I think the honest answer is that these models have partial, patchy world models. They're surprisingly good in some regions and then they fall apart in ways that a system with a coherent model shouldn't.

And that's actually the second kind of test I like, which is consistency. If a model really has a model of something, then it should give you consistent answers when you ask about it from different directions. If I ask it to describe the layout of a city, and then I ask it for directions between two points, those should agree. If it tells me A is larger than B and B is larger than C, it shouldn't then tell me C is larger than A. A lot of the failures we see in these models are exactly these consistency failures, where each individual answer looks plausible but they don't cohere. To me that's a signature of having learned a lot of local heuristics rather than a global structure.

A third thing is counterfactuals, and I find this one very informative. You take a situation the model handles well, and you perturb it in a way that's rare or absent from training data but that any system with a real model should handle trivially. Change the rules of a game slightly, change the gravity in a physics word problem, give it a map that doesn't look like any real map. Models that were just pattern-matching on familiar settings tend to break here. And the gap between in-distribution performance and the counterfactual performance tells you a lot about how much of what looks like understanding is really just retrieval.

I'll also say, coming from the computer vision side, I think this conversation is often too language-centric. A lot of what a "world model" should mean is about physical, spatial, temporal structure, and you learn a lot of that from perception, not from text. So when I look at multimodal models, I'm interested in whether the visual grounding actually improves these consistency and counterfactual tests, or whether it's just adding another modality of surface statistics. The evidence so far is mixed, honestly.

So to summarize how I'd assess it: don't ask the binary question. Pick a domain with known structure, probe the internals and do interventions where you can, test for consistency across different query types, and test on counterfactual variants that break the training distribution. And then you end up with a kind of map of where the model's world model is real and where it's an illusion. And I think that map is a much more useful thing than a yes-or-no answer.

opus-5.5.text:
That's a hard question, and I think part of the difficulty is that people mean different things by "world model." So I usually start by pinning down the definition. For me, a world model is an internal representation of the state of some environment plus how that state changes when things happen. If you have one, you should be able to predict what comes next, answer counterfactuals ("what if I had done X instead?"), and use it to plan. So the test is less about whether the model says correct things about the world and more about whether it has something internal that behaves like a simulator.

In practice I think about it at three levels.

The first is behavioral. You give the model situations where it can't just pattern-match, and you check whether its predictions stay consistent. You track objects through a long sequence of actions, change one detail and see whether the downstream answer changes in the right way and only in the right way, or pose physical and spatial reasoning problems in unusual configurations. A model that has memorized surface correlations often does well on the canonical version of a problem and falls apart when you perturb it slightly. A model with a real world model should degrade gracefully, because it's computing the answer from state rather than recalling it.

The second is representational. You look inside the network. The board-game work is the cleanest example: you train a model only on move sequences, and then you find you can decode the board state from its activations with a fairly simple probe. That tells you the information is there and organized in a way that mirrors the underlying state, even though the model never saw the board.

The third, which I find the most convincing, is interventional. Decoding the state isn't enough, because a probe might pick up something the model doesn't actually use. So you edit the internal representation, say flip a piece on the decoded board, and check whether the model's subsequent predictions change as if the world really were in that new state. If they do, you have causal evidence that the model is using that representation to compute its outputs.

My overall read is that current LLMs have partial, fragmented world models. In domains with rich, consistent structure in the training data, you can find surprisingly coherent internal state. But it's often local and brittle, not one unified model of the world. You see it in long-horizon tasks: the model keeps track of things for a while, then the state drifts and it contradicts itself. So I don't think the right question is a binary "do they or don't they." It's more like how much of a world model, for which domains, and how robust it is under perturbation.

One more caution, and it connects to some of my earlier work on datasets: evaluation itself is tricky. Many benchmarks that claim to test world understanding can be partly solved by exploiting biases in how the questions were constructed, or the content is already on the internet. So a lot of the real work is designing tests where the shortcut doesn't exist, because that's the only way to tell genuine modeling from very good interpolation.

fable-5.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and I think the honest answer is that it's actually really hard to assess, because "world model" itself is not a very well-defined term. So the first thing I usually do is try to make the question more concrete: a world model, to me, means the model maintains some internal representation of the state of the world, and it can predict how that state changes under actions or events — not just produce plausible text.

So there are a few ways people have tried to test this. One is probing studies — the classic example is the Othello work, where you train a model on game move sequences and then check whether you can decode the board state from its internal activations. That's evidence the model built up some state representation, even though it was only trained to predict the next token.

But for large language models, I think the more revealing tests are behavioral, and especially consistency tests. If a model truly has a world model, its answers should be consistent under paraphrasing, under reordering, under counterfactual perturbations. What we often find is that models do very well on questions stated the standard way, and then if you change the situation slightly — ask about an unusual physical setup, or compose two facts it clearly knows individually — performance drops a lot. That gap between in-distribution fluency and out-of-distribution consistency is, to me, the best signal of how much is genuine world modeling versus surface statistics.

My overall view is that it's not binary. These models clearly have partial, patchy world models — very strong in domains with lots of training coverage, and brittle elsewhere. So rather than asking "does it have a world model," I'd rather ask: for this specific domain, how far can the model extrapolate before its internal picture of the world falls apart? That's something we can actually measure.

opus-5.text:
Honestly, my first instinct is to push back on the question a bit, because "world model" is doing a lot of work and nobody agrees on what it means. If we can't say what observation would count as evidence against it, then we're not really doing science, we're just picking a vocabulary. So the thing I'd ask anyone making the claim is: what's the prediction, and what would falsify it?

Once you do try to operationalize it, the first problem you hit is that almost every benchmark is confounded by what's in the pretraining data. The internet is enormous. If a model answers physics questions well, the boring explanation — that something close enough was in the corpus — is usually not ruled out, and in my experience the boring explanation wins more often than people expect. So I care much less about scores on standard benchmarks and much more about controlled perturbations: take the same underlying structure and change the surface. Relabel the pieces, rotate the coordinate convention, flip one rule of the game, use units nobody writes in. If there's a real internal model, performance should degrade gracefully. What you often see instead is a cliff, which tells you the competence was riding on surface statistics.

The other thing I'd want is causal evidence, not just correlational. People find a linear probe that decodes board state from activations and call it a world model. Fine, but a probe only tells you the information is present somewhere. The stronger experiment is to intervene — edit that representation and check whether the behavior changes the way your interpretation says it should. If it does, that's real.

And then I think the honest answer is that it's not binary. It's coverage. Models clearly have something model-like in some regions and nothing in others, and the useful research question is mapping where the boundary is, not settling the yes-or-no.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think it first depends on what we mean by "world model," because people use the term in a lot of different ways. One meaning is that the model has an internal representation of how the world works, so that given a state and an action, it can predict what happens next. Another is looser: the model just behaves as if it understands physics, objects, and people. Those can come apart, so I'd separate them when evaluating.

The behavioral approach is the most straightforward. You give the model situations it is unlikely to have seen, especially counterfactual or out-of-distribution ones, and check whether it predicts consequences correctly. If it only does well on things that look like common internet text, that could be memorization or pattern matching. If it handles a new setup that requires reasoning about objects, causality, or other agents, that's better evidence. Consistency matters too: if I ask the same thing in different ways, or ask about the consequences of a consequence, does the model stay coherent?

The second approach is looking inside the model. You can probe the hidden states to see whether something like the state of the world is linearly decodable, as in the Othello work, where the board state seems to be represented internally. That's interesting, but a representation existing doesn't mean the model uses it. So I'd want causal interventions too: change that internal representation and see whether the output changes in the way you'd expect. Without that, you've only shown the information is there.

Even then, I'd be careful about treating "has a world model" as a yes-or-no question. It's probably a matter of degree and of domain. A model might have a quite accurate model of board games or simple physical scenarios and a very patchy one of something else. Its world model can also be a collection of heuristics that works in most cases and breaks in edge cases, which looks different from the clean, unified model we might imagine.

So my answer is to combine behavior on genuinely novel situations with internal evidence that is tied causally to the behavior, and to be specific about which world, and which aspects of it, we're asking about.

haiku-5.5.text:
That depends on what we mean by "world model." For me, the minimal bar is that the model keeps an internal state that tracks the structure of some environment and can use that state to answer questions it wasn't directly trained on.

I'd test a few things. First, behavior under distribution shift: if the model has learned the rules of a domain, it should handle novel configurations, longer chains of reasoning, and counterfactuals, not just the patterns it saw in training. Second, interventions: if you change the underlying state, does the output change the way the real world would? Third, internal representations. There's good work showing you can probe for things like board state in a model trained only on Othello move sequences, and that's suggestive. But being able to decode a feature doesn't mean the model uses it. You'd want to check causally, by editing the representation and seeing whether behavior follows.

I'm also skeptical of benchmarks that a model could solve with shallow heuristics or memorized surface statistics. A lot of apparent understanding falls apart when you rephrase the question or change the surface form. So my honest answer is probably "partially, and in a domain-specific way." The hard part is designing tests that separate genuine state tracking from very good pattern matching.

astra-6.text:
I think the first thing is to clarify what we mean by a world model. If we mean that a language model has learned some structure about how the world works, that seems plausible. But how rich is that structure, and when can the model actually use it? Those are harder questions.

One way I would approach this is to give the model a controlled environment where we know the rules. Then we can change something in that environment and ask it to predict the consequences. Can it keep track of the state over several steps? Can it handle a combination of events it hasn’t encountered before? Does it give consistent predictions when we describe the same situation differently?

Success on those tests would give us evidence, although I’d still be careful about interpreting it. A correct answer can come from several different strategies. Ideally, we would also examine the internal representations and test whether changing those representations changes predictions in the way we expect. That would help connect the model’s behavior to an actual mechanism.

I think we first need to be precise about what we mean by a world model. Being able to answer questions about the world is evidence, but it’s hard to tell how much of that comes from remembering patterns in the training data.

I would start with a controlled environment where we know the underlying rules. We can ask the model to predict how the environment changes after different actions, and then test it on situations or sequences of actions it hasn’t seen. Does it maintain a consistent understanding of the state? Can it use that understanding to plan? What happens when we change one of the rules?

Then I’d want to connect those behaviors to what’s happening inside the model. If we find a representation that appears to track something in the environment, can we intervene on that representation and change the model’s predictions in the way we expect? That would give us stronger evidence that the representation actually contributes to its behavior.

So I see this as a question of degrees. A model might capture some aspects of the world very well and fail on others. The useful thing is to identify what it represents, when that representation supports generalization, and where it breaks down.
